metaTitle: Ninja vs. Cosori Air Fryer (2026): Which Should You Buy?
metaDescription: Ninja AF181 Pro XL or Cosori TurboBlaze? We compare quarts, footprint, presets, max temps and what each maker discloses about PTFE in its basket coating.
h1: Ninja vs. Cosori Air Fryer: AF181 Pro XL or TurboBlaze 6-Quart?
answer: For most kitchens, the Cosori TurboBlaze 6-quart is the better all-rounder: nine presets, 90–450°F on every one, five fan speeds, more basket floor space and higher cooking scores from TechGearLab. Choose the Ninja AF181 Pro XL 6.5-quart for frozen foods on its fixed 450°F Max Crisp, an extra half quart and a clearer coating answer: SharkNinja lists no PTFE for units bought after January 1, 2025.

picks.why: Nine presets, a 90–450°F range on every one of them and five fan speeds give it far more control than the Ninja, and TechGearLab scored it higher for cooking. The catch: Cosori markets the coating as PFAS-free, yet its own California disclosure lists one version of this model with PTFE.

criteria.name: Cooking results in independent tests
criteria.explanation: Crispness, moisture and speed are why you buy an air fryer. We use TechGearLab's published scores and measurements (updated April 17, 2026), since it put both models through the same fries, tots, salmon and wings.

criteria.name: Temperature range and presets
criteria.explanation: A wide, adjustable range on every preset lets one appliance proof, dehydrate, roast and broil. We read the range and the function list from each maker's spec sheet and owner's guide.

criteria.name: Usable capacity
criteria.explanation: Quarts tell you volume; flat floor space tells you how much food fits in one layer, which is what crisps evenly. We weigh the maker's quart rating and the cooking area TechGearLab measured.

criteria.name: Coating disclosure (PTFE/PFAS)
criteria.explanation: Many US buyers want a PTFE-free basket. We rely only on what each maker publishes in its California cookware disclosure and on its product page, and on how easily a shopper can tell which version they're getting.

criteria.name: Footprint and weight
criteria.explanation: Counter and cabinet space are tight in most kitchens. We compare the makers' dimensions and weights, and the dimensions TechGearLab measured on the units.

criteria.name: Warranty and replacement parts
criteria.explanation: Baskets wear out before motors do. We compare the published warranty length and whether the maker sells a replacement basket and crisper plate for this model.

sections.h2: Ninja or Cosori: which one to choose
sections.html:
Choose the Ninja AF181 Pro XL if:

  • You cook mostly frozen fries, nuggets and tots. Max Crisp runs at a fixed 450°F, and Ninja's owner's guide recommends it for prepackaged frozen foods like fries and nuggets.
  • You want the extra half quart: Ninja rates the basket for up to 9 lb of chicken wings.
  • You want the simplest answer on the coating: SharkNinja lists no PTFE for AF18X units made after August 15, 2024 or bought after January 1, 2025.
  • You like six plain buttons and a slightly lighter unit (12.57 lb vs. 13.2 lb, by the makers' figures).

Choose the Cosori TurboBlaze if:

  • You want to set any temperature from 90°F to 450°F on any preset, including Proof, Dehydrate and Broil.
  • You often cook flat foods in one layer, like salmon fillets, cutlets or a full batch of wings: its square basket has more floor area.
  • You want the unit to shut off on its own when you pull the basket.
  • You want the longer warranty: Cosori advertises two years vs. one from Ninja, though its policy page labels the two-year term for California residents, so check the terms for your state.

sections.h2: Three differences you'll notice in daily use
sections.html:
• Temperature control. On the Ninja, only Max Crisp reaches 450°F, and you can't adjust it; Air Fry, Air Roast, Bake, Reheat and Dehydrate stop at 400°F, per the owner's guide. The Cosori lets you choose 90–450°F on every function, and its five fan speeds change with the preset (you can't set them yourself).
  • Basket shape. The Ninja holds more volume (6.5 qt vs. 6 qt), but TechGearLab measured more flat cooking area in the Cosori: 85.6 sq in vs. 74.8 sq in. If you crisp in a single layer, the smaller-rated Cosori fits more.
  • Pulling the basket to shake. Cosori says the TurboBlaze shuts off when the basket comes out mid-cook. Ninja's guide has you pause with the Start/Pause button, and TechGearLab listed the lack of a pause on basket removal among the Ninja's cons.

sections.h2: Footprint and capacity: 6.5 quarts vs. 6 quarts
sections.html:
Cosori lists the TurboBlaze at 11.8 x 14.4 x 11.9 in with its handle. SharkNinja's current page lists the AF181 at 16.3 x 12.6 x 14.17 in and 12.57 lb, noticeably larger than what TechGearLab measured on the unit itself (about 11.2 x 11.7 x 14.1 in, vs. about 11.7 x 11.5 x 14.2 in for the Cosori). In practice the two take up about the same counter space; if a cabinet opening is tight, plan for SharkNinja's bigger figure.

Leave room around either one while it runs: both push hot air out of vents, and Ninja's guide asks for adequate space above and on all sides for air circulation. Pull it out from under a low cabinet before you start cooking.

sections.h2: Presets: six on the Ninja, nine on the Cosori
sections.html:
The Ninja's six functions are Max Crisp, Air Fry, Air Roast, Bake, Reheat and Dehydrate. The Cosori adds Broil, Frozen, Proof and Keep Warm to Air Fry, Roast, Bake, Dehydrate and Reheat. Proof (90°F by default) and Keep Warm (170°F by default) have no equivalent among the Ninja's six functions, and the Cosori's Broil reaches 450°F where the Ninja's adjustable modes stop at 400°F.

TechGearLab found the Ninja's temperature steps awkward for dialing in a precise setting and liked the Cosori's top-mounted touch controls, with separate time and temperature adjustment. If you mostly press one button for frozen food, the Ninja's simpler panel is no handicap.

sections.h2: Nonstick coating: what Ninja and Cosori disclose about PTFE
sections.html:
PTFE is the classic nonstick fluoropolymer; Cosori's own disclosure page names it as an example of a PFAS chemical. Both brands publish the California cookware disclosure the state requires, and those documents say more than the product pages.

  • Ninja. SharkNinja's disclosure, the document its PFAS-info QR link opens, lists PTFE as the nonstick coating on AF180-series air fryers (the AF181 is part of that series) made before August 15, 2024. Its list for AF18X units made after that date, or bought after January 1, 2025, names metals and other chemicals but no PTFE. The owner's guide describes a ceramic-coated basket.
  • Cosori. The product page calls the basket and crisper plate “PFAS-free ceramic-coated.” Cosori's disclosure, updated April 15, 2026, lists the CAF-DC601-KUS under two SKUs: one ending in 161Y with PTFE among its chemicals, one ending in 161A without PTFE. The replacement basket and crisper plate appear in both versions too. The disclosure doesn't say how to tell them apart, so if PTFE-free matters to you, ask Cosori which version you're getting.

Under California law, cookware sold in the state with listed chemicals on food-contact surfaces must carry a “This product contains:” statement on the label. Check the box before you toss it.

The two draw almost the same power. At the US average residential rate of 18.16 cents per kWh (EIA, August 2026 data released October 23, 2026), a 20-minute cook at full rated power costs at most about 11 cents in either one; the heater cycles once the basket is up to temperature, so real use is lower. Five 20-minute cooks a week come to at most about $27 to $28 a year, and the gap between the two is under $1. Rates vary widely by state, so check yours on your utility bill.

The amperage matters more than the bill. Ninja lists 14.6 A; the Cosori's 1,725 W works out to about 14.4 A at 120 V. Kitchen outlets sit on 15 A or 20 A circuits, so running a toaster or kettle on the same circuit at the same time can trip the breaker. Ninja's guide also says not to use an extension cord.

Both makers sell replacement parts for these models: SharkNinja offers an air fryer basket and an AF180 crisper tray on the AF181's page, and Cosori's disclosure lists the TurboBlaze replacement basket and crisper tray (CRP-DC601RB-KUS and CRP-DC601RC-KUS). To make a basket last, follow the care notes: Cosori recommends warm water, mild soap and a non-abrasive sponge, and Ninja's guide rules out metal scouring pads.

Ninja covers the AF181 with a one-year limited warranty. Cosori advertises a two-year limited warranty on the product page, but its warranty policy, effective September 9, 2026, heads that term “California Residents Only” and doesn't say what applies elsewhere, so confirm the coverage for your state when you register.

• Cooking results (30): Cosori. TechGearLab scored it 79 overall vs. 75 for the Ninja, and 9.5 vs. 8.0 for fries and tots. The Ninja was faster on tots (19 vs. 22 minutes) and scored higher for temperature accuracy (8.0 vs. 7.0); set to 400°F, it averaged 408.5°F and the Cosori 391.6°F.
  • Temperature range and presets (20): Cosori. Nine presets with 90–450°F on all of them, vs. six presets with 400°F on all but Max Crisp.
  • Usable capacity (15): tie. More volume in the Ninja, more flat area in the Cosori.
  • Coating disclosure (15): Ninja. SharkNinja's cutoff by manufacture or purchase date gives a new unit a clear answer; Cosori lists one SKU of the same model with PTFE and one without, with no way to tell them apart in its disclosure.
  • Footprint and weight (10): Ninja, narrowly. Measured footprints are nearly identical, and the Ninja is lighter by the makers' figures.
  • Warranty and parts (10): Cosori, with a caveat. It advertises two years vs. one, though its policy page labels that term for California residents; both sell replacement baskets.

Weighted, the Cosori takes 60 points' worth of criteria, the Ninja 25, and 15 are tied. That makes the TurboBlaze our pick for most kitchens, and the AF181 the better buy if frozen foods and a clear PTFE answer come first.

• Two foods at once: the Ninja DualZone 10-QT Dual Air Fryer (DZ901) has two independent 5-qt baskets with their own fans and heaters, plus Smart Finish and Match Cook.
  • No nonstick coating at all: the Ninja Crispi 4-in-1 Glass Air Fryer cooks in 4-qt and 6-cup glass containers, which SharkNinja says are made without PFAS and PTFE. It's a smaller, different kind of appliance.
  • Check older Cosori models before you buy used: the CPSC recall of about 2 million Cosori air fryers (February 23, 2023) covered models such as the CP158-AF, CP137-AF, CS158-AF and CP258-AF. The TurboBlaze's CAF-DC601 isn't on that list.

We don't test products ourselves. We compared each maker's US spec sheet, owner's guide and California chemical disclosure, the results TechGearLab published for both models, and the CPSC recall database, all read on November 1, 2026. We checked that both models are sold new in the US. Specs and disclosures can change between production runs, so check the label on the box you receive.

faq.q: Is Ninja or Cosori better for an air fryer?
faq.a: Between their flagship single-basket models, the Cosori TurboBlaze 6-quart is the better all-rounder: more presets, 90–450°F on all of them and higher cooking scores from TechGearLab. The Ninja AF181 Pro XL is the better pick for frozen foods, a little more volume and a clearer PTFE answer.

faq.q: Do Ninja and Cosori air fryers have PTFE or PFAS?
faq.a: It depends on the unit. SharkNinja's California disclosure lists PTFE on AF180-series air fryers made before August 15, 2024 and none for units made after that date or bought after January 1, 2025. Cosori calls the TurboBlaze coating PFAS-free, but its disclosure updated April 15, 2026 lists one SKU of the model with PTFE and another without.

faq.q: Does the Ninja AF181 really reach 450°F?
faq.a: Only in Max Crisp, which runs at a fixed 450°F. Ninja's owner's guide puts the ceiling at 400°F for Air Fry, Air Roast, Bake, Reheat and Dehydrate. The Cosori TurboBlaze reaches 450°F on any of its nine functions.

faq.q: Which holds more food, the 6.5-quart Ninja or the 6-quart Cosori?
faq.a: The Ninja holds more volume, and Ninja rates it for up to 9 lb of chicken wings. The Cosori has more flat floor space: TechGearLab measured 85.6 sq in vs. 74.8 sq in, so it fits more food in a single layer.

No. The February 23, 2023 recall of about 2 million Cosori air fryers, announced by importer Atekcity, covered older models such as the CP158-AF and CP137-AF, sold from June 2018 through December 2022. A search of the CPSC recall database on November 1, 2026 found no recall of the TurboBlaze or of a Ninja air fryer; SharkNinja's May 1, 2025 recall covered Foodi multi-function pressure cookers.

faq.q: Do I need to preheat them?
faq.a: Ninja's guide recommends a 3-minute preheat on the AF181 before adding food. Cosori says preheating the TurboBlaze isn't always required but can make some recipes more consistent.

faq.q: Can I plug either one into any kitchen outlet?
faq.a: Yes, both run on 120 V, but each draws about 14.4 to 14.6 A. Don't run another heating appliance on the same circuit at the same time, and don't use an extension cord; Ninja's guide says so explicitly.
Yes. Both makers say the basket and crisper plate go in the dishwasher. For hand-washing, Cosori recommends a non-abrasive sponge, and Ninja's guide rules out metal scouring pads.

independentTesters.name: TechGearLab
independentTesters.note: The Best Air Fryers of 2026 (Lesley Robinson, updated April 17, 2026): the Cosori TurboBlaze scored 79 overall and was named best for families; the Ninja Pro XL 6.5 Qt scored 75. Fries and tots: 9.5 for the Cosori, 8.0 for the Ninja. Set to 400°F, the Ninja averaged 408.5°F and the Cosori 391.6°F (temperature accuracy 8.0 vs. 7.0); the Ninja cooked tots faster (19 vs. 22 minutes). Measured cooking area: 85.6 sq in for the Cosori, 74.8 sq in for the Ninja. Cons listed: a PTFE coating and food falling through the tray on the Cosori; limited temperatures, no pause on basket removal and no shake alarm on the Ninja, whose pros include no PTFE on the cooking surface.

independentTesters.name: RTINGS
independentTesters.note: RTINGS bought and reviewed both the Cosori TurboBlaze and the Ninja Air Fryer Pro XL AF181 and offers a side-by-side comparison (page read November 1, 2026). Its full results are for members, so we don't reproduce them here.
